title: When Cognitive Science Becomes a Checklist: The Problem with Generic Lesson Structures
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes argues that translating cognitive science into fixed, mandatory lesson structures - starter, explanation, questions, task, plenary - substitutes visible ritual for the professional judgement the research was meant to strengthen. Drawing on Roediger and Karpicke, Kirschner Sweller and Clark, Rosenshine, and Shulman's concept of pedagogical content knowledge, she argues each research finding is a principle to reason with, not a script to follow, and shows how a generic structure damages three different teachers in three different ways: the ECT learns to ask 'have I included retrieval?' instead of 'what does this class need?'; the experienced teacher hits a ceiling that blocks responsive adaptation; and the struggling teacher gains only the illusion of improvement while still choosing poor examples. She closes by arguing lesson planning should begin with the learning problem, not the phases of a template.
points: Hughes's central claim - that fixed lesson structures turn 'research findings become visible rituals... principles become phases... professional judgement becomes compliance' - is a sharp, citable critique of templated lesson design.

She grounds her critique in named research (Roediger & Karpicke on retrieval, Kirschner Sweller Clark on cognitive load, Rosenshine's principles, Shulman's pedagogical content knowledge) rather than a purely rhetorical argument.

Her three-teacher case study (ECT, experienced teacher, struggling teacher) shows how the same generic structure damages each differently - illusory security, an imposed ceiling, and false improvement respectively.

Her closing reframe of lesson planning - starting from 'what should pupils know... why is this difficult... what will I do if they do not' rather than fixed phases - offers a concrete alternative planning question set.
quotes: When cognitive science is translated into a fixed lesson structure, something important is lost. Research findings become visible rituals. Principles become phases. Professional judgement becomes compliance.

Kirschner, Sweller and Clark argue that novices usually need strong instructional guidance because unguided discovery can overload working memory. That is a powerful principle. It is not a command to place teacher explanation and modelling at point two in every lesson.

For an ECT, a structure may offer useful security at first, but if it becomes the measure of good teaching, it can prevent them from learning how to make principled decisions. They may learn to ask, Have I included retrieval and modelling? rather than, What does this class need to understand this concept?
For an experienced, effective teacher, the structure can become a ceiling rather than a floor. Over time, this shifts expertise from responsive decision-making to visible compliance.

A better lesson planning model would not begin with phases. It would begin with learning and learning problems. What should pupils know or be able to do by the end? Why is this difficult? What do they already know?
